summary: Gives operational guidance on running anycast services, where the same address is announced from several places for resilience and load spreading. It covers practices as services with high availability needs have grown. This is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Anycast lets multiple network locations offer a service at the same IP address. RFC 4786 explains how operators can manage routing, service health, monitoring and security when they do this.

questions: is anycast good for tcp services
subtitle: Operational guidance for providing one service address from multiple independent network locations.

tldr.problem: Services that need high availability can benefit from multiple service locations, but routing, monitoring, synchronization and security become more complex when several nodes advertise the same address.
tldr.mechanism: Anycast advertises a service address from two or more independent nodes. The routing system selects a node, and the RFC gives design and operational guidance for IGP and BGP deployments.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4786 is BCP 126. It describes a useful approach for selected services and smaller networks, while warning that route scaling makes global anycast unsuitable as a general service-distribution method.

today: RFC 4786 is Best Current Practice (BCP 126), published in December 2006. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Anycast Does
sections.content:
To provide a service with anycast, an operator associates it with a stable IP address and advertises reachability to that address from multiple, independent service nodes. The routing system chooses which node receives a packet based on the network topology and the request's origin.

The RFC is operational guidance for network operators. It applies to IPv4 and IPv6 and discusses both local distribution through an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) and global distribution through BGP. It does not recommend whether a particular service should use anycast.
sections.plainLanguage: Several nodes advertise the same service address, and the routing system chooses which node receives each request. This document helps operators plan and run that arrangement.

sections.title: Service Addresses, Nodes and Catchments
sections.content:
A Service Address is an IP address associated with a service. An Anycast Node is a connected collection of hosts and routers that provides the service at that address; an anycast system has two or more separate nodes.

A catchment is the part of the network whose packets are routed to one particular node. A Local-Scope address is visible to only part of the routing system. A Global-Scope address may be visible throughout that system.
sections.plainLanguage: An anycast node is one location that serves the shared address. A catchment is the network area whose traffic reaches that location.

sections.title: Benefits and Limits of Distribution
sections.content:
Anycast can spread load roughly across nodes, help contain some denial-of-service traffic near its sources, and provide redundancy. It can also make a service available through one address rather than a list of server addresses.

Load is usually uneven, and routing proximity does not necessarily mean a shorter round trip. A service needs to keep a client's transaction on the same node for its duration, so the stability of routing must be compared with the length of the transaction. Short exchanges can be easier to support than long downloads or streams.
sections.plainLanguage: Several service locations can provide redundancy and distribute some traffic. They may receive different amounts of traffic, and a route change during a long transaction can disrupt it.

sections.title: Choose a Suitable Service and Routing Scope
sections.content:
Before using anycast, operators should compare how long a transaction lasts with how stable the routing system is. The RFC gives short DNS transactions over UDP as an example of a brief exchange, and bulk downloads and media streams as longer transactions. A new protocol may separate setup at an anycast node from a longer phase at a non-anycast node.

An IGP is usually controlled by the organization operating the service, and can carry host routes directly. Across the global Internet, BGP routing policies are controlled by multiple organizations, and short covering prefixes may be needed for routes to propagate. The RFC notes that one route per service creates scaling and address-conservation costs, so global anycast does not scale as a general service-distribution method.
sections.plainLanguage: Use anycast only when routing is likely to keep a transaction at one node long enough. Local networks offer more operator control than global BGP, where route filters and route-table growth matter.

sections.title: Advertise Routes When Nodes Can Serve
sections.content:
A service node should be ready before it advertises reachability. When one route corresponds to one service address, the operator can tie advertising to service health and withdraw the route when the service becomes unavailable. Rapid advertise-and-withdraw cycles should be avoided.

Equal-cost paths to different anycast nodes can split packets from one transaction. The RFC notes that per-packet load balancing across links to different neighboring ASes can make a service unavailable downstream. In BGP, route flapping may be dampened; making the paths from different nodes diverse can reduce the chance that instability at one node affects the others.

For local-scope nodes, operators should use explicit route attributes or policies to constrain propagation. A route that escapes its intended area can overwhelm a node that was sized only for local traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A node should advertise a service route only while it can answer requests. Keep packet paths consistent during a transaction and use explicit routing policy to keep local routes within their intended area.

sections.title: Synchronize, Identify and Monitor Nodes
sections.content:
Service addresses must be unique within the routing system and chosen so their routes can propagate. Nodes should provide consistent answers when the service depends on shared data, so operators need an appropriate synchronization method. The RFC gives DNS zone transfers and rsync for FTP archives as examples, and says synchronization across public networks should use authentication and encryption.

To reduce cascading failures, nodes should be as autonomous as practical. A protocol can also identify which node answered, for example through an in-band identifier. Monitoring should use probes distributed across the routing system and record the answering node, because availability can differ by client location.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep data consistent across nodes and avoid making every node depend on the others. Monitor from different parts of the network and record which node answered each probe.

sections.title: Denial of Service and Route Hijacking
sections.content:
Anycast can spread denial-of-service handling across nodes and keep some attack traffic within a node's sphere of influence. Operating many nodes also increases monitoring and administration work, which can weaken security if it is not handled well.

An unauthorized party may advertise a route for the service address and capture requests. The RFC recommends robust authentication or integrity protection for services that require them. Operators also need working procedures to remove a compromised node quickly.
sections.plainLanguage: Anycast may distribute attack traffic, but an unauthorized route can send clients to a rogue node. Services that need identity or message protection should use protocols with strong authentication or integrity checks.
